projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with William McLaughlin was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Let's just start talking about where you were December 7th, 1940 --

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: One.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: -- one. So just repeat that. On December 7th, 1941 --

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: December the 7th, 1941, I'll never forget it. I'm over at 30th and Governor Printz Boulevard. And that was where the Wilmington Clippers had their ballpark they called Blue Rocks Stadium. And I never missed a game. That day I'm watching the Wilmington Clippers and Richmond play. And all of a sudden an announcement comes over this loud speaker and telling all of the servicemen to get back to their bases. And then it announced Pearl Harbor has been attacked. Well, that was the beginning of, you know, for me, spending four and a half years in the Air Corps, and it was just tremendous.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: What kind of day was it that day?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: It was a real nice day. It was a real nice day, you know. It was an ideal day for football.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Now, tell me your little story about when you heard Pearl Harbor --

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Oh --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: ___+ funny now.

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Oh, this is really something. I knew very, very little. I knew Hawaii, but I didn't know -- I knew very little aboutPearl Harbor. I didn't know there was a Pearl Harbor. When they announced that Pearl Harbor had been attacked, I thought it was some girl that had been attacked. And so I found myself finally over at Pearl Harbor when I was going over to the South Pacific. We stopped at Pearl Harbor.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Was it a regular Sunday? It was just a typical Sunday here in Wilmington?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: A typical Sunday, typical Sunday, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Cold? Sunny?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: It was just ideal for that time of the year.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Now, let's go on, and you tell me, okay, when you were at the game, what -- when you left -- you stayed until the game was over -- then what was your week like when you were hearing the news and you were hearing, like that night, I mean, was it on the radio here?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Oh, it was, oh, yeah, radio, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Just repeat back what --

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: I come home, and then I went to the radio right away, because I wasn't sure just what was happening. When I found out what really was happening, of course everybody was stunned -- they were in awe -- that how could this have happened to America and the Japanese, who had been our friends, you know, before that and everything like that. We were -- They were great trading partners with us. And all of a sudden they're attacking us. And the strange thing about it, if they had known how badly they had damaged us, they could most likely have taken Pearl Harbor that very, very same day. But they didn't know how badly they'd hurt us. And it wasn't long before -- I was working at a rug factory. It was during the Depression. I was working at the rug factory for 32 cents an hour. And it didn't take much for me to leave there and enlist in the Air Corps.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Did you go down that week? When did you --

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Oh, no, no. I waited quite awhile, close to my -- close to being drafted.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Which would have been what? Three months away? Two months? When did you go --

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: It was about -- It was about --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: It was December or so?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: -- five months away.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: So you went in, like, May?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Yeah. No. I went in in April.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: You went in in April?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Okay. Just tell me.

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: I went in in April.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: And where did you go?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: And they sent me to Fort Dix for the inauguration. And after that, they tested me, and they found out I was pretty good in radio. And so I became a radio operator and aerial gunner. And that's what I was on the plane, a radio operator and aerial gunner. Wind up going to Columbia, South Carolina, for my training, and then to the West Coast. We didn't know where we were going, you know. And they sent us to New Guinea, and when we got over there, we found out this woman was on the radio. Her name was Ann. Remember Tokyo Rose? Well, this was the same type of woman. Just telling us how foolish we were. We're over there. We're never going to get home again, because this is your last trip. And you're giving all this up for nothing, to defend a place like America, you know, how decadent we are and everything like this. It's really stunning. And the strange thing about it, she told us every stop, every island we went, and made you feel like there were ___ people looking at you then, you know. The Japanese had us surrounded. Well, when we got to New Guinea, we only had that one little place, Port Moresby, and New Guinea was one of the third largest islands in the world, very large. And the Japanese had all of it but Port Moresby.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: What kind of planes were you in? What was your squadron?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Medium bomber, B-25s, the Billy Mitchells. It's the same plane that they flew off the airplane carriers when they attacked Tokyo. So I don't know how they ever got those medium bombers off that plane, but they did.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Now, the command that you -- Why didn't you go to Tokyo at the time? Were you out? Were you --

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Oh, no.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Where were you guys, and where were you?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: All of that had already happened.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Oh, it had?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Sure, because one of the co-pilots of the pilot that was shot down -- the commanding pilot was shot down -- he wound up in our squadron. And so I got to know him. And he said one of the mistakes they made, his plane had crashed, and the pilot's name was Lawson. And he crashed the plane. And he had to land on the beach. He was supposed to land on the belly of the plane, and he had his wheels up because they were out of gas, you know. It was sort of a suicide mission they were making. And so he broke both his legs, the pilot did, but the co-pilot wound up in our group. He was okay.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Now, Columbia, South Carolina -- Now, Columbia, South Carolina is where they actually trained --

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Correct.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: -- these pilots, because they had a little air -- I was actually out there where they -- It was out towards Cecil Field where they actually --

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: -- had the mark-off for where it was a carrier and stuff?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: And they would learn to do stuff there, right?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Yeah, all that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Did -- What was Wilmington like right after -- right after -- right after Pearl Harbor? I mean, what was going on here in Wilmington? What was going on with your family? What was happening?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Oh, well I came from a family of 12 children. My mom and dad came over from Ireland the turn of the century and promptly had 12 children, like they had them all in one day, because we were so close together. And I had -- There were five brothers of us in the service at the same time and all in combat at the same time. And that's really unusual. One of my brothers who was working down in Washington, he was 15 years old. He lied about his age and got a job as a page boy down at Washington. When the war broke out, he knew he was going to get caught. By then he was working for the FHA, Federal Housing Administration. And he knew he was going to get caught. So he called me up and he said, "Bill, what should I do?" So I just joined the Air Corps. He said, "That's what I'm going to do." So he joins the Air Corps. He becomes an engineer, flight engineer, gets shot down his third mission, spends two and a half years in Stalag 17, the one they made the movie about and everything. They brought him up to Newark as part of that because he was one of the oldest of the prisoners of war. And he -- One good thing it did, it gave he and I an opportunity to go back to school, because both -- we'd quit school when we were, like, 16. He was only 15. He never spent a day even in high school. I at least spent one year in high school. It gave us a chance to get back to school under the GI Bill. And he, like, he graduated from the University of Delaware and then got his master's degree from Georgetown. Never spent a day in high school in his life. He went back to the Army in Army intelligence and spent the rest of his life there. And of course I was able to go in. And then I got married, so I had to quit the University of Delaware. So I spent ten years in night school while I was working for DuPont. I got a job in electronics in DuPont because of the break I got from the GI Bill. And, incidentally, that was one of the greatest things that ever happened to America, the GI Bill. It gave a lot of us the opportunity to get some education.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Take a little break, and -- Is that okay? How are we doing?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Videographer
sp.p: Very good. Looks good. The eye contact is good. His eyes sparkle.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Now, here again I want to get back to Wilmington. When I ask you these, sort of repeat what I'm asking you back. Back at Wilmington, the hustle and bustle that was going on here before you went off to war -- I know you were gone -- you were away from here for a while?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Four and a half years.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: But they had the Chrysler tank plant, correct, in Newark? Wasn't it Chrysler?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Uh-hmm.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: That they turned into a tank plant. DuPont was very big with the -- In fact, Governor Peterson was apparently on the, I guess, the experimental staff down in Seaford when they were making the actual cords for the parachutes. And apparently -- I mean, it was huge. But do you remember any of this? I mean, what was going on in Wilmington? Were they rationing yet before you left?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: No, none of that happened. They didn't exactly know what kind of trouble we were in. I mean, you know, you mentioned Governor Peterson. Well, he wouldn't -- When I was there he was working right at Tenth and Market with me. And I used to do some work for him in electronics. And he was -- he was head of research and development right here, and then they sent him down there. So Wilmington was a great town then. You know, even though it was a Depression, it was a lively town. A lot of great things were happening. And there wasn't a lot of work. As I told you, I was working for 32 cents an hour. You took whatever you could get. And they were drastic days, but they were also good days, heady days. The most important thing is no one ever explained to us that we were poor, so we never knew it. And these days everybody knows when you're poor and when you're not.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: What happened -- Do you remember the boom right at the beginning of the war? Was there a big boom with the ships down at the riverfront and stuff?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Oh, God, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Did the work start picking up?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Immediately, yeah. We did a lot of shipbuilding here. And a lot of women went to work there. And that's one that really got the women in the workfare, and they never forgot it. They kept right on working after the war.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Tell me about your brothers again. Tell me the different groups they were in. And tell me where you fit in with the five. So you can just say I was the third of seven brothers or the five brothers that went to war. Where did you fit in age-wise?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: I was the third. I was right in the middle, two younger and two older.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Where did they all go? Tell me --

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Well, we had one brother went in the Air Corps with me. Harry, my brother Harry, he was in the Navy. And the other two were in the infantry. One was a medic.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Are they still living today?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: The only ones that are living is Harry and I.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Where is Harry living?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Harry's down Rehoboth.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: He is. Oh, Harry was the --

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: State commander of VFW.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Harry was also the union rep?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Oh, yeah. He was --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: To the plumbers?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: -- the business agent for the Plumbers Union.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Now, what was Harry -- what branch was Harry in? Navy?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Navy.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: What did he do, do you remember?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: He was working on an oiler at one time. I know that. But he did a lot of different things. And he was in for four and a half years also.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Now, did all you brothers, did you go in all at the same time, or did one go? Who went in first? How can you recollect that? And here's the way you say it: Right after Pearl Harbor, we came back or we were getting ready to go to war, whatever. My oldest brother did this or -- How did that fit in?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Well, after Pearl Harbor, I was the first one to go in. And then Harry was only 18, and he joined the Navy. And then one of my brothers was working for Chrysler, and he had two children. They finally drafted him. And the other three were drafted -- the other two were drafted. Three of us joined, and two were drafted. They were in the -- Let's see. Two were in the Air Corps, one in the Navy, and two in the regular Army.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Did they go to Germany?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: All of them served overseas. Now, my brother was in Germany. He was in Army intelligent when he spent all those years in Germany. As I told you, his children spoke German.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Now, this is your brother that went in that snuck in and wanted to go in the Air Corps with you, right? He was working in Washington as a page?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Charles, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Charlie. Just say my brother Charlie -- Did he win a medal of --

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Oh, he won all kinds of medals. He, as I say, he was captured, and he had to parachute out of his plane. They were over Germany, and they were shot down. And they captured -- Farmers captured him first, and he thought that they were going to kill him. But they didn't. And then soldiers took him, put him in Stalag 17. He spent two and a half years in there. And then when he come out, he was living with me, and we both went back to school together on the GI Bill.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Now, how did they have the -- Tell me about the Sullivan brothers and how come you guy -- or that was after, I guess, they were all killed that they wouldn't allow --

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: They started that rule.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: And that was after you guys?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Oh, yeah, yeah. After the Sullivan brothers, they stopped putting brothers together like that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Did you ever hear that story, about the Sullivans, the five Sullivans who were all killed at the same time?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Videographer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: It was very tragic.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Videographer
sp.p: Different scenarios? Different --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: They were all on the same ship, weren't they?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Ship.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Videographer
sp.p: On the same ship?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Ship went down, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Yeah, and then they became -- It's the Sullivan Act or something that they had that none of the -- no blood relatives could be together --

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Right, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: -- on the same thing.

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Right, yeah, it's a good idea.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Okay. Let's see. I'm just trying to think what else. I think we pretty much covered it, huh?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Videographer
sp.p: Yeah, but now, since you're more conversational after the initial --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Let's do a --

sp.speaker: Unidentified Videographer
sp.p: Let's go back to the beginning, I would suggest.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Yeah, let's go back. Tell me again --

sp.speaker: Unidentified Videographer
sp.p: Ask how you learned about it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: How did -- What?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Videographer
sp.p: How he learned about Pearl Harbor and --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Yeah. Tell me again -- Tell me -- Let's go over Sunday, December the 7th, again, just for the sake of -- Take a little more water.

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: It was a great Sunday morning. Did you go to church then, and then you went over -- Who did you go to the ballpark with? Tell me the whole story.

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Well, in my family, you went to church first on a Sunday. You had to do that or you weren't allowed in the house.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Where did you go?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: St. Mary's church. We belonged there for many, many years. That's where we were married.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Videographer
sp.p: Just because you talked over him, maybe --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Okay. Let's just start again, and tell me when you got up that morning, and then you went -- Tell me the exact church you went to and what mass -- maybe if you can recollect that -- and then you called or you went over to Robbie's house, and then you went over to -- Just tell me about the day.

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Okay. I got up that morning. It was just like an ordinary Sunday morning. Had some eggs and bacon and then prepared to go to the football game. Went to mass first. Of course you had to go to mass in my house or you didn't live in that house. And it was just a typical morning. And a buddy of mine, Jimmy McCoggin (ph), he -- I call him up. We made plans to go to the game. We got over there. We're sitting there, and all of a sudden -- We're sitting there drinking beer, by the way. And all of a sudden they tell us about Pearl Harbor being attacked and for all the soldiers and sailors to get back to their bases. And that's all we knew. We didn't know anything about it, as I told you. I didn't know even where Pearl Harbor was. I knew where Hawaii was, but I didn't know where Pearl Harbor was.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Do you remember the inning? I mean, do you remember what quarter it was and -- if you can recall that? Were they winning at the time; weren't they winning at the time?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Yeah. It was -- I think it was around the third quarter, and they were playing Richmond, Richmond, Virginia, and -- who always had a good team. And they were winning a close game. And then all of a sudden this announcement comes over, you know, and it was telling us about Pearl Harbor being attacked and that all the soldiers and sailors had to get back to their bases and everything like this. As I told you before, I thought Pearl Harbor was a woman that had been attacked.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Did they stop the game, or did they continue with the game, or did they continue to play?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Oh, the game continued. And it took a little bit of edge off of it. There was no reason to stop the game. But then I didn't know any more until I got home, because nobody carried a little radio then. We just had the big Philco at home, and that's all there was to it, no TV or anything.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: How did -- How come you were drinking beer? How did you drink beer on Sunday? I didn't think they sold beer on Sunday.

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: We brought it with us.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: And you could do that?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: And you were all of how old?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: How old? Oh, we were -- I was -- I was 22.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Oh, were you?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Yeah. In fact, I was one of the oldest ones in my crew. Like when I was flying, I was actually around 24 and 25 years old, and my pilot was 22. He was a kid that went for Stanford and everything like this. I was the oldest one in the crew.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Videographer
sp.p: How was the radio broadcast?

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Tell me about the radio broadcast. You went home?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Oh, yeah. And of course it was -- it was over everything now, then. And then it told us in detail what was happening and how badly we were beaten there and everything. And we didn't know what was going to happen.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Because it would have been probably -- ___+ 6:00 at night. It would have probably still been around noontime?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: So you were at the game. You probably heard it around 3:00 p.m. in the afternoon?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Right?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: So that would have been -- three, six, nine -- God, it would have been --

sp.speaker: Unidentified Videographer
sp.p: I just find this very fascinating. I know that my father told me how he learned that in his family they were all against Germany starting the war. And then where they were all gathering around the tele -- the television -- radio, where they said we have attacked Poland in an act of revenge because the Polish --

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Videographer
sp.p: -- violated the integrity of the German border or something. And he told me the story of how his father was -- his stepfather and his mother, they were all sitting around and just then meeting the neighbors and discussing it.

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Oh, God, yeah. It had to have been an amazing thing for the people. You know, ordinary people think that, like, if you're German, you agree with Hitler.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: The vast majority of them didn't agree with Hitler.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Well, so let me see. I'm just trying to think. So you had been at the football game. Say there's six hours' difference. So at 3:00, say it would have been 9:00 there. So you got the news fairly quick?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: We did.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: A few hours. It was not like it was instantaneous, because I've done a little bit of reading on it. Now, when you got home and listened to the radio broadcast, which was probably 6:00 at night or so, which would have been probably 3:00 -- no -- which would have been noontime, probably, their time --

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: -- do you remember the -- Do you want to change --

sp.speaker: Unidentified Videographer
sp.p: No, no. I just --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Do you remember the announcer? Was it Walter Winchell? Was it -- Who was it, do you remember?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Oh, I don't -- No, I don't remember who that was.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Was your dad -- Was everybody there gathered around the set listening in?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Oh, God, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: When you got home, tell me what happened when you got home.

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: When we got home, of course my mother and father was thinking right away that all the sons they had would most likely be in the service. And it turned out five of us were in the service. But that's all people could talk about.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Now when you were gathered around the set, who was there? Do you remember who was there? And was your father saying anything about it? Was your mother saying anything about it?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: No. We were all just really listening, because we were sort of stunned that this could happen and because, you know, we were totally unprepared for that. In fact, we didn't have news then like we have now, like instantaneous news. But it was just totally amazing when you hear that man's voice and telling us what happened to us, and we didn't know what was going to happen after that, whether they were going to follow through or Germany was going to attack us or what. We didn't know what was going to happen. It was really strange, when I went into the Air Corps, I did my training down in Miami, Florida. We took the hotels over down there. And how totally unprepared we were. They made us, like, patrol the beaches. But we didn't have any guns. And I had a piece of stick like a rung of a chair. I was walking -- And the real shore patrol, they would just laugh at us every time we passed them. But they just made us do it, you know, to give us some instance of what we were going to be faced with.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: And was it radio school down there? What was going on down there? Where did you go to radio school?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Oh, no. I went to St. Louis to a radio school, and -- St. Louis, Missouri -- and learned radio procedure and everything like that. It was really strange. There was a fellow in my class. I looked at him. I said doggone it, I know him, and everything. And then it just dawned on me it was Clark Gable. He joined as a, you know, as a private. He didn't take any -- because he was -- He was a big guy then, you know, in the movies. And there he was sitting there taking radio with me. It was really amazing.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: How did you get your -- So you went in to Fort Dix first?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: You got your basic training there?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Basic training at Fort Dix.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: And you were actually in the Army then?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: And then you split off and went to the Corps, correct --

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Yes, uh-hmm.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: -- air? Okay. So you went to Fort Dix, and then you went from Fort Dix to St. Louis? No.

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: No. I went to Columbia, South Carolina.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Fort Jackson.

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: And then they sent us to radio school.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: When did you know --

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: We had to take some tests.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: -- you were going to be in the Air -- So tell me: You went to Fort Dix. Then you went to Fort Jackson, South Carolina.

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: I knew I was going to be in the Air Corps before Dix because they picked 25 of us. They gave us tests. And the 25 that passed the test, they put us in the Air Corps. Later on, the gunnery training and all came later.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Where did you have your training? What did you at Fort Jackson?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Well --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: When you say Fort Jackson, Fort Jackson, South Carolina.

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: No. I was at Columbia Army Air Base, Columbia Army Air Base.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Which is out where the airport is now?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Oh, okay. So I was at Columbia -- What did you do at Columbia, South Carolina?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Well, we -- we -- We learned to fly with a crew and everything like this, because the pilots were starting new and everything like this. In fact, there's a possibility we could have lost as many people in training as we did in the war, because B-25s and B-26s, medium bombers, are very difficult to fly. So there's a lot of accidents.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Videographer
sp.p: What is this noise? A train?

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: No. Are you hearing it? It sounds like, you know, an air conditioning unit.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Videographer
sp.p: A train over a bridge.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Air conditioning unit.

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: You know what that is? That's a heater.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: And tell -- With Clark, did you ever follow through with Clark Gable at all, I mean, when he was at school? Did you --

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Oh, no, no. Well, while I was at school yeah, we'd hang out a little bit together, you know, at night and things like this. But he was just an ordinary guy. It just stunned me because he was the biggest movie star we had then. And usually, you know, the rest of them, they got commissions and everything like this, and they didn't do much, you know. Like Ronald Reagan, they made him a captain or something, and all he just did was a commercial sort of like thing. But he just went in as a private.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Still trashing the Republicans.

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: No. It wasn't that -- The --

sp.speaker: Unidentified Videographer
sp.p: It's true.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: No. Tell me about -- Tell me about after the war, when you got back.

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Oh, after the war --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: What year? What was going on here? Were you -- Where were you on, like, VJ Day or V -- D-Day?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Interesting. VJ Day. After I come back, they assigned me to a base in Austin, Texas, and so -- Because I was one of the early returnees, all they had to do was teach one class a day one hour a day, so I had all that free time. So I signed up at the University of Texas for some courses. And that gave me a big start and everything like this, because the government paid for all that. And then of course I resumed it at the University of Delaware. But we had a football team, and we played a college schedule. So I was a radio operator and aerial gunner or -- rather -- radio operator on this, and we played a sched -- We played the University of Iowa, and we played the University of Texas. And the University of Texas then had an all-American quarterback. What the hell was his name? I'm trying to think of it. But, anyway, he became an all-pro and everything like this. So we played them. And they beat us seven to six. We had a lot of ex-football players from Notre Dame and everybody. And that was my job, when the war ended, the football schedule was still going on, so I stayed three extra months to complete the football schedule. But when we finally ended, what we were doing, I had an assignment where we were working with paratroopers. And we were flying this plane, and the paratrooper would jump out of the plane. And for their final -- their final jump would be in Havana, Cuba, and that's where they jump from. So I made about six or seven trips down to Havana, Cuba. And I was in Havana, Cuba, when the war ended, and they wouldn't let us leave. It took us six extra days being down there before they'd release us to come back to the United States, because things were in confusion. So I spent the last six days down there in Havana, Cuba.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: When did you come back to Wilmington? What was -- You stayed there for three months, right, three more months down in Texas?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Yeah, uh-hmm, stayed three extra months in Texas. And you had to have points. At one time I was in this airplane, and the Japanese Zeros were the fastest planes there were, no doubt about it, and they would -- They were the fighter planes. And when they'd attack you, they'd like to come right down your throat, you know. And I was a waist gunner. I'd leave the radio and then take up my gun. And one time this flak hit right in front of me, and I jumped back, and I hit my head on one of the rafters and put about nine stitches in my head. When you come back, they debrief you. They give you a couple of shots of whiskey, and then they'd debrief you. And then they put nine stitches in my head. Now, they wanted to give me a Purple Heart for this, but I said, man, I don't want to explain that. I said I jumped away from my gun, for God's sake. Because I was so scared, I said, I just jumped back and hit my head, and that's how I got that. So you can get a Purple Heart for that. If I'd known you got five points towards getting out, I would have taken it, but I didn't want to have to explain this the rest of my life, how I got this Purple Heart. I left my gun.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: How many combat missions did you fly?

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Well, tell me: I flew --

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Well, I flew 50 combat missions.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Videographer
sp.p: Excuse me please. I was not really on you. I didn't follow you fast enough. Can you just repeat. Just start over how many combat missions you flew. I'm sorry.

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Oh, when you complete your 50 missions, it doesn't mean you go home.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: No. Tell me a little bit about your 50 missions, saying I completed 50 -- How many missions did you complete?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: I completed 50 missions, was shot down once, and luckily we landed in our own territory, and we were picked up in a short period of time. But there was no big problem there, so we were okay.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Well, tell me where you crash landed, meaning an island or in the water or whatever you did, and what happened after that? How did that work?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Well, we crash -- We came in on our belly because our landing gear had been shot out, and we couldn't -- we couldn't get our landing gear down. And we knew we were going to have to crash somewhere. And so luckily we got in our own territory when he saw the first open field. And all the time I'm on the radio giving our position, you know, to tell them where we are and close enough to where they could find us. And so he crashed it in on the belly of the plane, and we were all picked up. Nobody got hurt.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Where was it?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Oh, this was -- We'd hit Rabaul. Rabaul in New Guinea was their largest city. And the strange thing about it, you know, in 9-11 when you saw all those people running down the street? That's what this mission reminded me of, because we hit Rabaul. It was so fortified the government -- or General MacArthur bypassed it when he had gone to the Pacific because it was so well fortified. He just isolated them in the city. But I remember us going down, and we were low level bombers. We bombed in strafe. We could see people running down the street, innocent people, and we just dropped the bombs on them anyhow. That's the way we did it. That's what it reminded me of when I saw 9-11. It just reminded me of that mission I was on and how horrible war is.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Did -- Tell me about your first mission. And when I'm asking you these, repeat: My first mission was -- And tell me where. Was it out of New Guinea? Were you flying out of New Guinea? Where were you going on, like, your first mission?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Well, my first mission, the strange thing we were also going to hit Rabaul. That was their most fortified city. And what scares you the most is, like, they wake you up around 4:00 in the morning, and they take you in this briefing. And then they show you where all the enemy guns are. And then you're looking at, oh, my God, all these enemy guns and everything, and we get to fly right in the face of that and everything. And I -- The things I used to hate the most is those kind of briefings.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Did you stay with the -- Did the whole crew sort of stay together for your all 50 missions?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: We only lost one -- We only lost one gunner during our 50 missions. He was killed.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: In your plane?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Yeah. He was shot right in the plane, yeah. An enemy plane -- One of the Zeros came in.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Do you remember what mission that was? And tell me a little bit about that. Where were you flying?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: That was about our 24th mission.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: So tell me: On our 24th mission we were flying to bup (ph), and then, you know, bup-bup, and then coming back or when you were attacked by the Zeros. So on our 24th mission --

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: On our 24th mission we were going to Lae, L-a-e. We were going to hit that. And that is when one of our gunners was killed. A Zero just come in and just hit us hard and killed him. He never survived. He was killed instantly. But that's the only casualty that we had. We didn't have anybody was even wounded outside of him. So we were lucky.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Did you have a lot of cover from the Navy and the Marines, the air guys?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: We always -- We always had a lot of cover, according to where we were going to be, who the cover was going to be. But, you know, we had P-38s, P-45s, and things like that. Our planes were really fortified. Our planes could get hit and come back. The Japanese planes like the Zero, if you got a good hit on them, they just disintegrated. They depended on speed, and we depended on getting -- being able to hit and still survive the mission.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Was there -- There was a lot of, I know, Navy or -- Navy or Marine guys over there that were flying the Corsairs, the F-8s --

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: We --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: -- out of those islands. Did they ever help you?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: None of them. No, none of them helped. We were -- We were on an invasion once, invasion of New Britain. It's right off the coast of New Guinea. And General MacArthur flew this mission with us, although he was about 50,000 feet, and we were down about 15,000 feet. But we were supposed to come in and clear the beach off before the Marines could come in. And before we could get to our target -- and it's all timed -- before we could get to our target, the Japanese fighters attacked us and so held us up. We had to make all kinds of maneuvers and everything. So we got there. The Marines had already landed. But we went in and dropped our bombs, killed a lot of Marines. We killed -- They shot down our commanding officer, and they wouldn't release him. They were so furious at us. And they shot down three of our planes, and the Japanese didn't shoot any down, but the Marines shot three of our planes down. And that was just one of those human errors that you make during the war.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Interesting. What do you think?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Videographer
sp.p: I think it's really fascinating to listen to all this.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Should I tie anything in of -- I'm thinking about passing on to other generations, to sort of end this or to sort of --

sp.speaker: Unidentified Videographer
sp.p: Yeah, sure. I think this is a very good interview.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Take some water.

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: You're going to have a hard time editing this.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Oh, no. This is good. Because we've got a lot of really good stuff. I mean, I'm happy with what I have. I mean, I don't -- Do I need a couple profound statements?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Videographer
sp.p: What comes to your mind when ___+ still -- Is there anything that we didn't ask? Is there anything that you want to tell us?

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Right. Is there anything that you -- about the war or about --

sp.speaker: Unidentified Videographer
sp.p: Interesting side story or --

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Here's something interesting. I don't know if you could use this or not. Remember I told you we dropped the bombs on the United States Marines? It turned out -- I don't know if you knew who Johnny Williams was or not, another bookie in town. One time he worked for Joe Dahlin (ph). But he joined early, and he became a Marine. He became a Marine. And he went through all the islands, you know, fighting and everything like this. And the strange thing, he was on that invasion of New Britain, and we didn't know. I went to visit him in the hospital when I come back, and we start comparing notes. And he started telling me. I said, "Oh, my God. We dropped bombs on you." And he was on that invasion. Didn't get hurt, but he was on that invasion.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Is he still around?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: No. He died. Every friend I ever had did.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Now, is he here in Wilmington? Did he go to -- Was he -- What happened to your buddy that you were with that day -- did he join up? -- at the Clippers game?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Oh, yeah, yeah. He -- In fact, he joined up with me. And we were in -- Jimmy McCoggin, yeah. He worked at the Bancroft Company back then, yeah, right down here. And he joined with me. He was quite a heavy drinker. And he'd get me in a lot of trouble, because I'd wind up taking him home, you know. And we were in the service and everything like this. In fact, one time I got him home, and he went like this and everything and smacked me right in the eye, gave me a black eye, you know. I get up the next morning and explain to my captain what the hell happened to me.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Was he in the same squadron?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: No, no, no. We separated. He didn't go in the Air Corps. And he went in -- He went in the regular Army.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Was there anybody else that was in that -- in your squadron that was from here?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: No?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: No one.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: I think that's it. When you got married down in St. Mary's and Father Enright (ph)?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Oh, my God.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: I've got to get this on camera.

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Mary and I lived a block from each other, my wife, my girlfriend then. We lived a block from each other. But we never really went out until after I come back from the service. And then we were 30 years old when we got married. So we were going to get married at St. Mary's church. Father Enright was the pastor. And that afternoon we were supposed to get married 2:00 in the afternoon Notre Dame and Army were continuing their rivalry that was stopped during the war. And so he was all set to go to the Army/Notre Dame game, Father Enright was, big Notre Dame fan. So when he found out we were getting married there and everything, we walked in the church, and he said, "Bill, do you think Mary would mind, and if I pulled the radio up close to the altar, we could listen to the game?" I said, "No. She loves football." She hated football. Anyway, we could hear Notre Dame playing Army during the mass. And Mary still thinks to this day she's married to Johnny Lujack, who was a quarterback of Notre Dame back in those days.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: That's funny. Now, what did -- Tell me what Mary -- What did Mary do during the war? Did she do anything?

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: No. She was a -- She worked at Dover Trust Building. When I first met her, she was working at Dover Trust Building. She was working in the office.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: She didn't do USO stuff or --

sp.speaker: William McLaughlin
sp.p: Well, all those girls did all kind of things like that and everything. But the strange thing about it, the biggest mistake of my life, we were married about -- maybe about seven or eight months, and I'm working for DuPont, right, and I had never called her at her office. So for some reason that day I had to give her a call. I gave her a call. And her supervisor got on the phone and gave me a lecture about bothering her girls and everything like this. So she went on and on. I said, "Well, okay, now, will you do me a favor? Will you go down and tell Mary McLaughlin she just quit." And she -- she never went back to work. Worst mistake I made in my life. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: I think it's good.
